source.title: V-FIND: Revealing the Intrinsic Forgery Knowledge Encoded in Video Forgery Detectors
source.authors: Shi-Chao Kan; Chengpeng Hong; Jing-Tong Dou; Chuan-Cheng Shi; Yuhan Liu; Linrui Xu; Yi-Xiong Liang; Yi-Gang Cen; Yan-Peng Sun; Fei Shen; T. Chua

record.tranche_reason: The study analyzes forgery-discriminative neurons in video detectors, but does not measure whether individual neurons respond to unrelated input types or test any listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The study reports neuron selection and intervention results for real-versus-forged video discrimination. Those results concern task-specific forensic function, not whether neurons mix unrelated meanings, so the rows are linked to none of the claim versions. Benchmark results for detector performance are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study selects forgery-discriminative units in frozen video forgery detectors and tests them with activation swaps. It never measures whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs, how common that is, or what causes it. Zoom In is cited only as background on neuron interpretability. It neither tests nor relies on polysemanticity, so cites_only/T6 fits better than discusses.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that forgery-discriminative knowledge in video forgery detectors sits in a sparse set of functionally specialized neurons. They describe it as extractable and reusable with a frozen backbone and a linear readout, and cite intervention results as evidence of functional specificity.
record.recipe_differences: V-FIND localizes layers using real/fake representation discrepancies, selects neurons using probe-weighted response effect sizes, and tests LANs with activation swaps; it is not the original claim's analysis of mixed semantic responses.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports changes with layer interval, neuron-selection threshold, selected-neuron count, discovery-set size, input-frame count, training-data size and input perturbation strength. These sensitivities concern detection performance, not polysemanticity measurement.

fits_no_version.finding: Swapping the activations of the 211 selected LAN units shifts real/fake decision logits about twice as much as a same-layer random set. Label-flip rates rise from 6.8% to 19.7% (Fake→Real) and from 1.2% to 1.8% (Real→Fake).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a frozen Qwen2.5-ViT video forgery detector, a sparse probe-selected set of units carries a stronger causal effect on real/fake decisions than budget-matched random units. This says nothing about whether those units are mono- or polysemantic.

record.problems: Intervention outcomes are reported for the LAN set collectively, not as a survey of individual neurons' responses to varied semantic inputs. The authors also note they do not systematically investigate closely related detector variants or consistency across checkpoints, scales and backbone variants. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the intervention results.
record.rows_left_out: Detector benchmark results, layer-localization scores, threshold sweeps, training-data-size results and other robustness results were left out because they measure detection performance or selection settings, not whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs.

untested.parts: The study does not survey whether individual ViT neurons respond to unrelated visual inputs. Its Figure 4 response maps show only forgery-related texture and boundary cues.
No language-model MLP neurons are studied.
Superposition and capacity are not tested.
Initialization, regularization and training noise are not tested as causes.
The cross-architecture results (VINA, X-CLIP) measure detection accuracy, not the share of polysemantic neurons.
The study does not revisit canonical polysemantic neurons.
The study does not compare activation ranges or explanation scoring for classifying neurons as polysemantic.

record.verdict_notes: Relation was changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only'. The paper only cites Olah et al. 2020 in its related work and never engages with polysemanticity. The claim of 'functionally specialized neurons' is about task relevance of a selected set, not single-meaning neurons. Single-unit monosemanticity is never tested, so it should not be read as evidence against V1 or V2.

versions.untested_parts: Does not examine image-classifier neurons responding to multiple unrelated visual inputs.
Does not study language models, token/context polysemanticity, or its prevalence across layers.
Does not test superposition or whether feature capacity exceeds neuron count.
Does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity under sufficient capacity.
Does not compare activation functions, architecture or regularization for their effect on polysemanticity, or assess the cost of reducing it.
Does not revisit canonical polysemantic neurons or determine whether their mixed inputs share a feature.
Does not compare measurement ranges or explanation-scoring methods for classifying neurons as polysemantic.

rows.note: Reported as the mean shift for LAN intervention compared with a budget-matched, same-layer random control; measures forgery-decision function, not response to unrelated input meanings.
rows.check: The row measures the decision-logit shift from swapping the 211-neuron LAN set against a random set. That is the study's own method compared with a control, not a polysemanticity measure. Relative to the claim versions the state is cannot_determine. 'Observed' only holds for the study's own question.
